story: I bought a mixer grinder for Rs 3,200 online on 5 October 2026. It was broken. I returned it on 8 October but they have not refunded me.

timeline.event: Bought a mixer grinder for Rs 3,200 online

evidence: Online purchase receipt for Rs 3,200 (5 October 2026)
facts.user_goal: To get a refund of Rs 3,200 for the returned broken mixer grinder

rules.name: consumer_limitation
rules.message: File your consumer complaint before 05 Oct 2028 (697 days left). This counts 2 years from 05 Oct 2026 (your purchase date - counted from the earliest possible day, to be safe). Don't wait for the last date. Sending a letter or calling the helpline does NOT pause this clock.

facts_used.start_basis: purchase date (earliest possible start, to be safe)

rules.label: Last date to file your consumer complaint

rules.name: forum_and_fee
rules.message: You paid Rs 3,200, so the complaint goes to the District Consumer Commission, with no filing fee. You can file in the district where you live or work, online at e-jagriti.gov.in. You don't need a lawyer to file.
rules.label: Where to file

rules.name: free_first_steps
rules.message: Two free steps often work first: (1) a written complaint to the seller's or platform's grievance officer, (2) the National Consumer Helpline: call 1915 or WhatsApp 8800001915.
rules.label: Try these first

answer.summary: You bought a mixer grinder online for Rs 3,200 and returned it because it was broken. The seller has not given you a refund. You can file a consumer complaint to ask for your money back.

claims.text: You are a consumer because you bought goods for personal use.
A broken item is a 'defect' in the goods.
The seller's refusal to take back a broken item and refund you is an unfair trade practice.
You can file your complaint with the District Consumer Commission because the amount paid is below Rs 50 lakh.
There is no filing fee for a complaint up to Rs 5 lakh.
You must file your complaint within two years of the purchase date.

next_steps.action: Call the National Consumer Helpline at 1915 or WhatsApp 8800001915.
next_steps.why: This is a free first step to try and get your refund without filing a formal case.

next_steps.action: Send a written complaint to the seller or the online platform's grievance officer.
next_steps.why: This creates a paper trail and shows you tried to resolve the issue directly before going to court.

next_steps.action: File a complaint online at e-jagriti.gov.in.
next_steps.why: You do not need a lawyer, and there is no filing fee for your case.

questions_for_user: Did you receive a return confirmation number or email from the seller or platform?
Did you contact the seller or platform to ask for a refund after returning the item?
Do you have the online receipt and return confirmation saved?
not_covered: This does not cover what to do if the seller claims they never received the returned item.
This does not cover criminal fraud complaints.

support.text: You are a consumer because you bought goods for personal use.
support.reason: The law text defines 'consumer' as any person who buys goods for consideration (paid or promised, including deferred payment), and explicitly includes 'any user of such goods other than the person who buys such goods' when used with approval. Buying goods for personal use falls within the definition of buying goods for consideration.

support.text: A broken item is a 'defect' in the goods.
support.reason: The law text defines 'defect' as 'any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard' required by law, contract, or claimed by trader. While a broken item may involve a fault/imperfection, the law text does not explicitly equate 'broken item' with 'defect' - it requires the fault to relate to quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard. 'Broken' is not synonymous with these specific attributes in the definition.

support.text: The seller's refusal to take back a broken item and refund you is an unfair trade practice.
support.reason: The law text explicitly defines unfair trade practice (viii) as 'refusing, after selling goods or rendering services, to take back or withdraw defective goods or to withdraw or discontinue deficient services and to refund the consideration thereof.' A broken item would constitute 'defective goods', and refusal to take back and refund fits this definition.

support.text: You can file your complaint with the District Consumer Commission because the amount paid is below Rs 50 lakh.
support.reason: The law text states 'District Commission: consideration paid up to Rs 50 lakh.' This establishes the jurisdiction threshold, but the sentence adds a causal connection ('because the amount paid is below Rs 50 lakh') as the reason for filing with District Commission. The law text only states the amount limit; it does not say this is the sole or determining factor for jurisdiction, nor does it explicitly link 'below Rs 50 lakh' to being able to file there as a complete rule. More critically, the law text says 'up to Rs 50 lakh' which is inclusive, while the sentence says 'below Rs 50 lakh' which is exclusive of Rs 50 lakh - a subtle but important difference that could affect whether exactly Rs 50 lakh is covered.

support.text: You can file your complaint with the District Consumer Commission because the amount paid is below Rs 50 lakh.
support.reason: The law text provides multiple jurisdictional bases for filing a complaint with a District Commission (residence/business of opposite party, cause of action arising, complainant's residence/work). It does not mention the amount paid as a factor for District Commission jurisdiction. The sentence adds a monetary condition that is not in the law text.

support.text: You can file your complaint with the District Consumer Commission because the amount paid is below Rs 50 lakh.
support.reason: The law text lists who may file a complaint (consumer, recognised consumer association, multiple consumers with permission, government authorities). It does not mention the amount paid as a criterion for who may file. The sentence adds a monetary condition that is not in the law text.

support.text: There is no filing fee for a complaint up to Rs 5 lakh.
support.reason: The law text explicitly states 'No fee where the consideration paid is up to Rs 5 lakh.' The sentence states 'There is no filing fee for a complaint up to Rs 5 lakh.' This matches directly.

support.text: You must file your complaint within two years of the purchase date.
support.reason: The law text states complaints must be filed 'within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen' (s.69(1)), and allows condonation of delay if sufficient cause is shown (s.69(2)). The sentence says 'You must file your complaint within two years of the purchase date' - this changes 'cause of action' to 'purchase date' and omits the possibility of condonation of delay. The law text does not say 'must' in an absolute sense, and the time trigger is 'cause of action', not 'purchase date'. The sentence adds conditions (absolute 'must', purchase date as trigger) not in the law text.

draft_notes:
How to send it:
1. Find their correct address in the invoice, order page, or the seller's 'grievance officer' details on the website/app.
2. Fill every [FILL] slot. Remove anything that isn't true - only state facts you can prove.
3. Send by Speed Post and keep the receipt and the tracking proof of delivery. Also send a copy by email or WhatsApp and keep a screenshot.
4. Wait 15 days. Sending this letter does NOT stop any legal time limit - file your claim/complaint before the deadline shown, even if they haven't replied.
5. Free help to check the letter: legal aid 15100 or Tele-Law 14454.

Laws this letter relies on: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.69 (Two-year limitation and condonation); Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.34(2) (Where to file: District Commission); Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.35(1) (Who may file a complaint; e-filing)
